title: Metro 2039 gameplay trailer looks like bad news for your aging graphics card
summary: My gut says a regular PC will not like this game.
body: The latest trailer for Metro 2039 tried to get a scare out of me with its radiation-sickened bugs and monsters jumping at the screen, but the spookiest thing about it is how gosh darn good it looks. I'm not talking specifically about the gameplay, which this trailer does show more of—gun customization, mask wiping, stealth kills, the Metro hits—but the graphics. 4A has always been one for graphical showpieces (Metro Exodus was an early adopter of full ray tracing), but Metro 2039 is a significant step up in the realm of photoreal. It's got that high-frequency detail and soft lighting that, at times, makes outdoor spaces look like straight-up photographs. Which begs the question: will a normal person's computer be able to run this thing? That question wouldn't usually be top of mind, except, well, we're deep into a hardware crisis that shows no signs of stopping. Powerful PC hardware is almost impossible to reasonably obtain, a sad reality that has some of us embracing the great Tech Pause . title: The hardware crisis has hit a new low: We're now using rats for RAM
summary: Rat computer.
body: Good news from the near future: Space travel has apparently advanced enough to allow humanity to establish a hotel on the surface of the moon. Bad news: The RAMpocalypse apparently continues unabated, forcing novel experimentation with alternate forms of computer memory not rendered wholly unaffordable by AI datacenters. Namely, rat computers. This believable projection of the current miserable state of consumer hardware comes courtesy of Ontos, the next game from Amnesia developer Frictional Games. In the trailer above, a man strapped to a chair with electrodes stuck in his head is a bit freaky, though less so than another guy who's missing everything from his upper teeth down; perhaps humanity in the future is so desperate for localized processing power that we're resorting to shoving DisplayPort cables into our brains, too. The strongest big of imagery in the trailer by far, though, is a computer the size of a wall with 60 rats connected to it in sequence. Or parallel? I'm not great on my circuitry fundamentals, but I know a rat computer when I see one. title: Atari is taking another shot at reviving RollerCoaster Tycoon
summary: RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks is being developed by Springloaded, makers of the excellent Let's Build a Zoo.
body: Last we saw RollerCoaster Tycoon it was in pretty rickety shape. More than a decade after RollerCoaster Tycoon 3, the follow-up—RollerCoaster Tycoon World—was released to nearly universally poor reviews. Even worse, in one of the all-time dick moves in gaming industry history, Atari launched it exactly one day before rival sim Planet Coaster was due to release. Wow. That nakedly desperate move didn't help the situation: people liked Planet Coaster and didn't like RCTW, and the Tycoon series has been silent since 2016. But here we are another decade later, and Atari is bringing RollerCoaster Tycoon back yet again—though I'm already feeling more hopeful about it. RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks was announced at Gamescom today, and the new entry in the series is being developed by Springloaded, who made the excellent Let's Build a Zoo and is releasing promising gamedev sim Let's Build a Dungeon later this year. That's a good sign, at least! There's no date on the books yet, and RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks won't be feature complete when it launches: it's "coming soon" to early access. We got our first look at Warlock gameplay at Gamescom's Opening Night Live showcase today. Check it out above. body: Nvidia's new DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction feature is laser-focused on trying to fix the second most annoying thing about ray traced or path traced games: visual artifacting. Yes, the lighting effect does deliver the most accurate-looking lighting and shadows in games, but in motion there is a definite visual weirdness added into scenes. And that weirdness generally comes from the denoising pass designed to turn the low-fidelity path traced image, with its limited number of rays, into a fully realised frame. Leave a game's viewport still and the scene will pretty rapidly come together to make a sharp, convincing image. Shift that around, or have that scene filled with moving objects or characters and you're going to see the sort of visual trails you might only have been used to in the warehouse parties of your early twenties. Just me? The issue is that it's way too expensive in terms of raw compute to trace every single photon/pixel that would otherwise make up a fully traced scene.
